body.text: Across social media platforms, Karakalpak activists have increasingly found themselves on the wrong side of copyright and other complaints, leading to the removal of content and the disabling of profiles.

Recently, an unknown person presenting themselves as an editor for The Diplomat filed at least one fraudulent copyright complaint, which led to the removal of a post on Facebook. This one case is illustrative of a wider weaponization of copyright law, its uneven application, and the abuse of automated reporting systems to target activists.

“We are losing more than accounts and audiences,” Gulya Nur, a Karakalpak activist and president of the Via Serica Foundation, told The Diplomat. “We are losing documentation: testimony, interviews, records of abuse, and years of civil society work. After silencing outspoken people through repression inside Karakalpakstan, pressure on online voices threatens the remaining space for documenting and challenging that repression.”

On October 31, Nur contacted The Diplomat. A fellow activist, Aman Sagidullayev, had shared the text of an op-ed Nur had written, which was published by The Diplomat. Sagidullayev’s post had been reported to Meta as a copyright violation and Meta removed it, notifying Sagidullayev of the details of the complaint and his appeal options.

Sagidullayev is the leader of the Alga Karakalpakstan movement. In exile since 2012, his movement has long demanded a referendum on independence in Karakalpakstan. The autonomous republic – and the people who would like to see it attain complete independence – have a complex history with Uzbekistan, to say the least.

In the summer of 2022, a draft version of a then-proposed constitutional referendum was published. The draft scrapped an article that guaranteed Karakalpakstan the right to secede from Uzbekistan on the basis of a referendum. That perceived attempt to chip away at Karakalpakstan’s sovereignty sparked protests and a renewed crackdown. The constitutional referendum that passed in April 2023 retained the clause that the draft had cut. But although Karakalpakstan’s right to secede is technically still a constitutionally-guaranteed right (now under Article 89), in practical terms discussing it remains a taboo.
The notice Sagidullayev received from Meta stated that “The removal decision was made by our technology.”

Social media sites like Facebook use automated systems to assess content for violations, including copyright. Such platforms are motivated to move quickly, as failing to act expeditiously in response to a sworn takedown notice opens them to legal liability under the Digital Millennium Copyright Act (DMCA) in the United States. The law includes what’s known as a “safe harbor” provision that shields platforms from liability if they make a good-faith effort to respond to complaints. Automated systems speed up this process, but shift the burden onto the user to file a counter-notice when content is wrongfully taken down.
Sagidullayev has appealed Meta’s decision to disable the post.

When you file a DMCA complaint with a platform like Meta, which operates Facebook and Instagram, you attest under penalty of perjury that the information in the claim is accurate and that you are the copyright owner or authorized to act on their behalf. Under U.S. copyright law, only the legitimate copyright holder, or their authorized agent, has standing to file complaints.

As noted above, platforms are motivated to move quickly in response to complaints. As such, they do not assess the complainant’s standing to make the complaint in the first place before taking steps to remove content. This inadvertently opens the door for imposters to silence individuals using tools designed to protect copyright.

The complaint against Sagidullayev was submitted by an individual referring to themself as Jasmina Jasurova. In response to the form’s prompt inquiring how the affected work was infringed, the complainant wrote:

“I, Jasmina Jasurova, am an editor at The Diplomat (https://thediplomat.com/). The two reported fake profiles repeatedly steal and republish our editorial team’s original content without authorization, seriously infringing our copyright. I urge Meta to immediately remove all infringing content and take strict enforcement action against both profiles, including permanent removal, to prevent further violations.”

As managing editor of The Diplomat since 2017, and on staff since 2014, I can state with complete confidence that no person named “Jasmina Jasurova” has ever worked as an editor for The Diplomat. When The Diplomat contacted the email address used to file the complaint (a Gmail address), we did not receive a reply. Google searches of the name in English, Uzbek, and Russian yielded nothing significant.

The Diplomat has sought ways to file a counter-complaint with Meta, but there appears to be no mechanism by which a copyright holder can complain directly about an unknown individual impersonating them in making a DMCA takedown request. There are forms for copyright and trademark infringement, and forms for reporting accounts that may be impersonating another account and other abuses. But while we have the name and email address used to file the complaint, we do not know what Facebook account they are associated with – Meta does not provide that information. There are several dozen Jasmina Jasurovas on Facebook.

Questions sent to Meta’s press office inquiring about whether the company has systems in place to ensure that only legitimate copyright holders are able to file complaints and what mechanisms there are for redress when a fraudulent complaint is filed and acted upon went unanswered as of publication.

This is not Sagidullayev’s first run-in with copyright complaints. His YouTube channel “Civil Society of Karakalpakstan” was terminated following multiple copyright strikes. Many of those complaints appear to have been submitted under an email address bearing his own name, according to documents viewed by The Diplomat.
Sagidullayev told The Diplomat he has already lost previous Facebook accounts, “and, with them, my connection to thousands of followers.”

“It hurt to lose touch with people who counted on me for information about Karakalpakstan. Through those accounts, I helped people harmed by Uzbekistan’s authorities tell their stories and be heard,” he said. “I’m asking Meta to restore my previous accounts. If it shuts down my current profile, I could lose years of human rights documentation and once again lose contact with the people who rely on my work. It takes minutes to open a new account. It took years to build that archive and earn that trust.”
Jasmina Jasurova, the complainant fraudulently posing as a Diplomat editor, asked for a permanent removal of his account from the platform.

“Uzbekistan’s security forces used bullets and grenades to silence peaceful protesters in Karakalpakstan. Now Uzbekistan authorities are weaponizing Facebook and YouTube to silence the Karakalpak voices online,” Sagidullayev told The Diplomat. “I believe Uzbekistan’s security services are behind the repeated shutdowns of my Facebook accounts.”

Other Karakalpak activists have similarly reported being targeted with copyright complaints, sometimes even for reposting their own material to different platforms. Activists like Sagidullayev and Nur believe they know the source of these complaints, but hard evidence is difficult to come by given layers of online privacy rules and the use of sock puppet accounts.
Uzbek authorities have long denied targeting critics, at home or abroad.
This comes at a time when Uzbekistan, like many countries, is making a concerted push to invest in and expand its digital sphere.
“As Uzbekistan promotes digital cooperation abroad, Karakalpak defenders struggle to preserve their voices on those same global platforms,” Nur told The Diplomat.

In June 2026, Uzbekistan’s Minister of Digital Technologies Sherzod Shermatov met with Beth Ann Lim, director of public policy, strategy and campaigns for the Asia-Pacific (APAC) region at Meta, “to discuss the development of Uzbekistan’s digital economy, the expansion of bilateral cooperation, and the advancement of digital skills among young people,” according to a government readout.

“These partnerships deserve scrutiny alongside the use and potential abuse of platform complaint systems,” Nur argued. “American technology companies should be asking how their services protect people documenting repression.”

Nearly a decade ago, Freedom House highlighted “the rise of digital authoritarianism” in their 2018 Freedom of the Net report. “Digital authoritarianism is being promoted as a way for governments to control their citizens through technology, inverting the concept of the internet as an engine of human liberation,” the report warned.

Scholars summarize digital authoritarianism as the “use of digital information technology by authoritarian regimes to surveil, repress, and manipulate domestic and foreign populations.” Discussions of digital authoritarianism often focus on mass surveillance and control of information. This ranges from propaganda and disinformation – muddying the waters with false but neatly packaged narratives – and repressing authentic voices through “fake news” laws and the criminalization of defamation.

But this also includes the weaponization of copyright to achieve goals unrelated to copyright, such as censorship and retaliation. Tools designed to protect copyright can be easily deployed for ulterior purposes by a range of actors, from individuals to governments the world over, and ultimately shift the boundaries of public discussion. The very platforms that provide the avenues for free speech also provide the tools of repression. It’s a dark irony to be wrestled with.
